title: Probability Adventure 3: Exam-Style Stretch
welcome_lead: Stretch time! You'll handle without-replacement trees, expected frequency, and complementary events.
meta_desc: GCSE Maths Probability stretch — without-replacement trees, conditional probabilities, expected frequency, complementary events.
final_note: You can build without-replacement trees, use expected frequency = P × n, and apply P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

concepts.def: Item kept out, so totals change for the next pick
Probability that depends on what happened first
An event and "not the event" — they sum to 1
Equals 1 − P(A), the chance A does not happen
Often easier as 1 − P(none of them)

walkthroughs.body_html:
If you do not put the first item back, the totals shrink. The second probability is conditional on the first.

Example: 5 red and 3 blue counters (8 total).

  • P(red 1st) = 5/8
  • If red was drawn, now 4 red and 3 blue remain (7 total). P(red 2nd | red 1st) = 4/7

P(red, red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14

If you repeat an experiment many times, how often do you expect an event?

Expected frequency = P(event) × number of trials

Example: a fair dice rolled 60 times. P(rolling a 6) = 1/6.

Expected number of 6s = 1/6 × 60 = 10.

This is an estimate — actual results will vary.

Every event A has a complement: "not A". Together they cover every possibility.

P(not A) = 1 − P(A)

This is brilliant for "at least one" questions. P(at least one six in two rolls) = 1 − P(no sixes) = 1 − (5/6 × 5/6) = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.

mcqs.q: When picking WITHOUT replacement, what changes for the second pick?
options: The totals shrink, so probabilities change

mcqs.q: If P(A) = 0.8, what is P(not A)?

numericals.q: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn WITHOUT replacement. What is P(red, then red)? Give the answer as a decimal.

free_texts.q: A spinner lands on green with probability 0.3. If spun 200 times, what is the expected number of greens? Number only.
free_texts.hint: Expected frequency = probability × number of trials.
